blocks.text: Words That Make People Act

Imagine two businesses selling the same product at the same price. One converts at 2%, the other at 8%. The difference isn't the product, the design, or the ad budget. It's copywriting.

Throughout this course, you'll learn how to write the kind of copy that turns interest into action using AI to work faster, test more, and scale what works. 

Let's get started!

feedbackCorrect.text: The pricing page drives plan selection, the ad drives a return purchase, the email drives a booking, and the "About Us" page shapes brand perception. All of them serve a business goal. Copywriting encourages action. It doesn't have to sell directly; it can also promote a company, a product, or an idea over time.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Copywriting covers any writing that serves a business or marketing goal, whether that's a direct sale today or building trust that leads to action later. A Wikipedia article is neutral, factual reference content with no persuasive or promotional intent at all.

blocks.text: What Is Copywriting?

Copywriting is writing that serves a business or marketing goal — it persuades, promotes, or positions a company, product, person, or idea to drive action. That action can be immediate (buy, subscribe, sign up) or long-term (trust, loyalty, brand perception).
It's easy to confuse copywriting with related forms:

• Content writing, which focuses on delivering standalone value — think blog posts, tutorials, or guides. It may build trust, but the piece itself isn't structured around a business action.
  • Creative writing, which expresses ideas, tells stories, or entertains without a commercial goal.
Copywriting can also educate and build trust, but in the service of a business outcome. A product page might teach you how a feature works, but the goal is to move you toward business-related action.
Copywriting Is Everywhere

Every ad you scroll past, every email subject line that makes you click, every "Buy Now" button — someone wrote that. Copywriting powers landing pages, product descriptions, email campaigns, social media ads, and sales pages.

Wherever a business needs to turn attention into action, there's copy behind it.
Why AI Changes Everything

Before AI, writing great copy meant long manual research, drafting, rewriting, and hoping for a breakthrough. It was slow, and it relied heavily on individual talent and experience.

AI flips that. Now you can generate a first draft in seconds, produce dozens of variations, and test different angles — all before your morning coffee.

But a more valuable shift is in scope. AI can help you at every stage of the copywriting process: researching your audience, shaping your strategy, drafting copy, critiquing what you've written, and rewriting to make it stronger.

You're still the one making decisions — but now AI can guide and support you through the entire process.
From Research to Revision — Where AI Fits
To see where AI creates the biggest advantage, let's map out what a copywriter's job looks like beyond just "writing." The full process has distinct stages, and AI can play a role in each one.

Before any writing happens, a copywriter needs to research — understand the audience, the market, and what competitors are saying. AI can analyze competitor copy, surface audience pain points from reviews, and summarize market trends.

Next comes strategy and planning — defining the offer, choosing an angle, and deciding the format. AI can help you brainstorm positioning options, generate multiple angles for the same offer, and outline content structures based on proven frameworks.

Then there's writing and iteration — the draft-and-revise cycle where raw ideas become polished copy. This is the stage most people associate with copywriting, and it's where the core workflow you'll learn next makes the biggest difference.

Finally, there's testing and optimization — generating variations for A/B tests, adapting copy for different platforms, and refining based on performance data. AI can produce dozens of headlines or CTA variants, giving you more options to test than you could write manually.

Now that you've seen the full map, let's zoom in on the stage that ties it all together — writing and iteration. There's a specific system for turning raw AI output into effective copy, and you're about to try it yourself.

feedbackCorrect.text: True! Without context about the audience or key benefit, the AI is guessing — and so are you when picking from the results. Generating volume without direction rarely produces strong copy.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Getting 10 options feels productive, but none of them are focused. There's no audience, no goal, no way to judge quality beyond gut feeling. A better approach starts with giving AI specific direction before generating anything.

blocks.prompt: Arrange these steps in the correct order of the best workflow sequence.
blocks.title: The Copywriter's Workflow

blocks.text:
The workflow consists of the following steps:
  • Brief: Set the direction before you prompt. Define your audience, goal, tone, and format.
  • Draft: Use AI to produce a first working version based on your brief.
  • Critique: Identify the strongest and weakest parts of the draft against clear criteria. What's working? What's weak?
  • Rewrite: Tell AI exactly what to fix and how, so each pass makes the copy measurably sharper.
blocks.title: Your Workflow

blocks.text: This reliable workflow helps you build a system based on intentional iteration. Let's see it firsthand.

blocks.exampleResponse: "Upgrade your mornings with our premium coffee blend. Made from the finest beans, our coffee delivers a rich, smooth taste you'll love. Order now and experience the difference!"
blocks.prompt: Try generating copy with a simple, quick prompt.
blocks.template: Write [copy type] for my [product]

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! "Finest beans," "rich, smooth taste," and "experience the difference" could apply to any coffee. There's no specific audience, no unique benefit, no emotional hook. This is what happens when you skip the brief.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Having a product mention and a CTA is a starting point, but this copy could belong to any coffee company on the planet. It lacks specificity — who is it for? What makes this coffee different? Generic prompts produce generic copy every time.

options.label: Yes, it mentions the product and includes a call to action
No, it's generic and could describe any coffee brand

blocks.question: Is this copy ready to use?

blocks.exampleResponse: "You don't need a café to start your morning right. Our single-origin Ethiopian blend is roasted in small batches for people who care about what they drink — but not about wasting time. Bold, clean, ready in 3 minutes. Subscribe and never run out."
blocks.prompt: Now apply the brief → draft approach. Fill in the details to give AI proper direction.
blocks.template: Write a product description for [service]. Target audience: [audience]. Key benefit: café-quality, fast. Tone: [tone]. Include a call to [action].

feedbackCorrect.text: True! Specificity is the key. When you define audience, benefit, tone, and desired action, you give AI constraints — and they produce focused, relevant copy.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Prompt length doesn't guarantee quality, and ChatGPT doesn't learn between separate prompts. The improvement came entirely from giving specific context — audience, benefit, tone, and CTA — which narrowed the AI's focus and eliminated the generic filler.

options.label: ChatGPT learned from the first attempt and improved automatically
The second prompt was longer, and longer prompts always work better
The brief gave AI a specific context, so there was less room for generic filler

blocks.question: Why did the second prompt produce stronger copy?

blocks.text: Great Work!

Now you see the difference between "generate and hope" and a brief-first approach. You moved from asking for "a description" to giving real direction — and the writing instantly became more specific and persuasive.
AI in the Critique & Rewrite Stages

The critique step is where most people underuse AI. Instead of just rereading your own draft, you can ask AI to evaluate it against specific criteria: clarity, specificity, emotional pull, and CTA strength. It gives you a second perspective instantly, helping you catch weaknesses you might overlook.

For the rewrite, the key is giving AI targeted instructions — not "make it better," but "the CTA is vague, rewrite it with a specific outcome and a time constraint." The more precise your rewrite instruction, the sharper the next version. This is how iteration compounds: each pass fixes one thing, and the copy gets measurably stronger.
The Copywriting Foundation

You now know what copywriting is, where it shows up across business, and how AI applies to every stage. You've also practiced the brief → draft → critique → rewrite workflow and seen firsthand how a specific brief transforms generic AI output into focused, usable copy.
Your Next Steps

blocks.text: The Right Tool for the Right Job

There's no single "best" AI tool for copywriting. Each has a task type where it consistently outperforms the others. Knowing these strengths lets you pick the right tool before you start, instead of wrestling with the wrong one.

Let's dive deeper into each tool's capacities and the best use cases.
ChatGPT

ChatGPT is the most flexible general-purpose AI tool. It's strong at brainstorming, exploring angles, and thinking through strategy — when you're not sure what direction to take, ChatGPT helps you figure it out through back-and-forth conversation.

blocks.exampleResponse:
1. Time-saving — "Stop meal prepping for hours." Parents are exhausted; removing effort is the fastest emotional win.
  2. Health without sacrifice — "Eat clean without thinking about it." They want to do right by their family but don't have the bandwidth to plan.
  3. Family approval — "Dinners your kids will actually eat." The real barrier isn't cooking — it's picky eaters.
  4. Budget — "Cheaper than takeout, better than frozen." Guilt about spending on convenience is real.
  5. Identity — "You're a good parent. Dinner shouldn't be the proof." Reframes the emotional stakes entirely.
blocks.prompt: You have a new client, but aren't sure which angle will resonate. Use ChatGPT to think through the options.
blocks.template: I'm writing ads for [product type] targeting [audience]. I'm not sure which angle will work best. Give me [number] different ad angles, each focusing on a different motivation this audience might have. For each angle, explain briefly why it could resonate.

blocks.text: You just used ChatGPT to think through a problem before writing anything. This is where ChatGPT shines — exploring directions, testing angles, and building strategy through conversation. Whenever you're stuck on what to say, start here.
Claude

Claude excels at long-form writing, nuanced copy, and brand voice adaptation. blocks.text:
Effective copywriting prompts consistently include these five elements:
  • Audience: Who is this for?
  • Goal: What action should the reader take?
  • Key benefit: What specific value does the reader get?
  • Tone: How should it sound?
  • Format and constraints: What length, structure, or platform rules apply?
Missing any of these forces AI to guess — and AI guesses with clichés.

blocks.text: Building Your Prompt Library

Writing a detailed prompt every time you start a new task works, but it's slow. Professional copywriters solve this by building a prompt library: a collection of reusable prompt templates for the tasks they do most often.

A prompt template is a prebuilt structure with placeholders you replace for each project. Instead of crafting a prompt from scratch, you fill in the blanks — audience, benefit, tone, offer — and get a consistent, high-quality starting point.

blocks.exampleResponse: Email Subject Line Template: "Write a subject line for *campaign type* promoting *offer* to *audience*. Trigger: *emotional hook*. Max *characters*." Quality check: Does this subject line give a specific reason to open, or could it apply to any brand? Landing Page Hero Template: "Write a hero section for *product*. Audience: *audience*. Benefit: *benefit*. Tone: *tone*. Include headline, supporting line, and CTA." Quality check: Could a visitor tell exactly what this product does and who it's for within 5 seconds? Short-Form Ad Template: "Write a *platform* ad for *product*. Angle: *reason to care*. Audience: *audience*. CTA: *action*. Max *characters*." Quality check: Does the hook match the awareness level of the audience — or does it assume they already care?

blocks.template: Create [number] reusable prompt templates for these copywriting formats: [format], landing page hero sections, and short-form ads. For each template, add one quality-check question I can use to evaluate whether the AI output is strong enough.

blocks.text: Excellent!

Notice what makes these templates specifically useful. The quality-check questions turn each template into a self-correcting system. To check whether an AI output is good enough, you have a specific question to evaluate it against every time. As you take on more projects, keep adding templates and refining the ones that work best.

blocks.question: What do you think a copywriter needs to define before writing anything?

blocks.text: The Three Foundations of Effective Copy
Every piece of persuasive copy rests on three elements:

• A clear offer: What are you selling and to whom?
  • A defined audience: Who are you writing for, and what do they care about?
  • A credible proof: Why should anyone believe your promise?
Let's explore each of them!
Start With a One-Sentence Offer

Before you open any AI tool, you need to answer one question: What exactly are you offering? A one-sentence offer defines the product, the audience, and the core outcome in a single, clear statement. If you can't say it in one sentence, your copy will be unfocused — and so will every AI prompt you write from it.
Compare these two:

• Vague: "We help businesses grow with our platform."
  • Clear: "We help e-commerce brands recover abandoned carts with automated email sequences that average 12% conversion."
The second version tells you who it's for, what it does, and what result to expect. That's a one-sentence offer.

correctTokens: a meal planning app called Mealwise
weekly meal planning taking too long
blocks.exampleResponse: Mealwise is a weekly meal-planning app that gives busy parents a personalized grocery list and 30-minute dinner recipes tailored to their family's dietary needs — cutting weekly food planning from 2 hours to 10 minutes.
blocks.prompt: Use Claude to sharpen a vague product idea into a focused one-sentence offer.
blocks.template: My product is [product]. It's for [audience] who struggle with [core problem]. Help me write a one-sentence offer that clearly states who it's for, what it does, and what specific outcome it delivers.
tokens: a meal planning app called Mealwise
weekly meal planning taking too long

blocks.text: Great!

Notice how much work that single sentence does: it names the audience, the product, the mechanism, and a measurable outcome. Every piece of copy you write for this product can now point back to this sentence for direction.
The Message Triangle
A one-sentence offer gets you started. To build copy that convinces, you need three elements working together — what we call the message triangle.

• Offer: What are you selling and to whom?
  • Outcome: What specific result does the reader get?
  • Proof: Why should they believe you?
Every strong piece of copy answers all three questions. Weak copy is almost always missing one.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! The offer is there (AI writing tool), and the outcome is stated (10x faster). The missing piece is proof — what makes "10x faster" credible? A stat, a case study, a specific mechanism. Without proof, bold claims feel like marketing noise.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The offer is present — "AI writing tool" tells you what the product is. "10x faster" is an outcome — it tells the reader what they'll get. The problem isn't that the outcome is weak; it's that there's no evidence to back it up. Speed is a clear benefit, but without evidence (a user study, a comparison, a concrete mechanism), the reader has no reason to believe it. Proof is what turns a promise into a persuasive claim.

options.label: Proof — there's no reason to believe the "10x faster" claim
Outcome — "10x faster" isn't specific enough to count as a real outcome
Offer — it doesn't say what the product costs

blocks.question: "Our AI writing tool helps you create content 10x faster." Which element of the message triangle is missing?

blocks.text: Types of Proof
Proof doesn't always mean testimonials or case studies. There are several types you can use depending on what's available:

• Social proof: user numbers, reviews
  • Process proof: explaining how or why something works
  • Specificity proof: concrete details that signal credibility ("847 teams" feels more real than "hundreds of teams")
  • Constraint proof: what you don't do ("We only work with B2B SaaS" signals expertise)
The more specific the proof, the stronger the trust.

correctTokens: a sleep coaching app called NightOwl
blocks.exampleResponse:
Offer: NightOwl is a sleep coaching app that builds personalized wind-down routines for adults who can't fall asleep without screens. Outcome: Users fall asleep 25 minutes faster within the first two weeks, without medication. Proof:
  1. Specificity: "Built on 12 peer-reviewed sleep studies."
  2. Social: "Used by 15,000 people in the last 6 months."
  3. Process: "The app adapts your routine nightly based on your sleep data."
blocks.prompt: Use Claude to build a complete message triangle for a product — offer, outcome, and proof.
blocks.template: Build a message triangle for [product]. Define the offer in one sentence. State the primary outcome for [audience]. Then suggest [number] types of [evidence] that would make the promise credible.
tokens: a sleep coaching app called NightOwl

blocks.text: Excellent!

You now have a repeatable structure for preparing any piece of copy. Define the offer, state the outcome, then choose the proof that makes it believable. This triangle will feed directly into every brief you write going forward.
Audience Research With AI

Your message triangle answers what you're saying. Audience research answers who you're saying it to — and how to say it in a way that resonates. AI can accelerate research dramatically. Instead of spending time reading reviews and forums, you can prompt AI to surface pain points, desires, objections, and language patterns.
Pain Points and Desires
Strong copy connects these two things:

• Pain points — the specific frustrations, problems, and obstacles your audience faces right now.
  • Desires — the outcomes and the future state your audience is trying to reach.
Building Audience Personas

The next step after recognizing pain points and desires is organizing that knowledge into a profile you can write to. An audience persona is a detailed profile of your ideal reader that goes beyond demographics. Personas give you a specific person to write to, which is why you'll produce sharper, more emotionally relevant copy.

blocks.exampleResponse: Name: Sarah, 34, marketing manager. Frustration: Spends Sunday evenings dreading the inbox she didn't clear on Friday. Tried: Todoist, sticky notes, blocking time on the calendar — none stuck. Secretly wants: To feel in control without thinking about productivity. Main objection: "Another app won't fix my habits." Her words: "I don't need more tools, I need fewer things on my plate."
blocks.prompt: Use ChatGPT to create a detailed audience persona based on a target market.
blocks.template: I'm writing copy for [product] targeting [audience]. Create a detailed persona including: their biggest frustration, what they've already tried, what they secretly want, their main objection to buying, and the exact language they'd use to describe their problem.

blocks.text: Notice the last section — "her words." That's the most valuable part. When your copy uses the same language your audience uses to describe their problem, it feels like you're reading their mind. AI can quickly surface this language, and you can validate it against real reviews and forums.

You can dive deeper into the audience language research. Use ChatGPT: paste in actual reviews or forum quotes and ask it to find patterns — the words and phrases that repeat across multiple people. When your copy mirrors that language, it creates instant recognition: "This is exactly my problem."
Audience Psychology in Your Prompts

Understanding your audience goes beyond demographics. Psychology principles help you tap into the emotional drivers behind decisions — and you can embed these principles directly into your AI prompts.
These three principles show up in effective copy because they tap into fundamental human decision-making patterns:

• Loss aversion hits hardest when your audience is already experiencing a cost. Lead with what they're losing.
  • Social proof works best when your audience feels uncertain or is comparing options. Numbers and peer validation reduce perceived risk.
  • Urgency and scarcity accelerate decisions when the reader is already interested. A deadline or limited quantity pushes them past hesitation.
The key is choosing the principle that matches where your reader is emotionally, not stacking all three at once.

feedbackCorrect.text: "Join 5000 marketers" suggests that many others have already made this decision successfully. It reduces risk and makes the reader feel they're joining a proven group rather than taking a chance alone.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Loss aversion focuses on what the reader stands to lose if they don't act. This line leads with what thousands of others have already gained — that's social proof, building trust through numbers and shared outcomes.

blocks.instruction: Which principle is being used in this copy line?

options.label: Social proof
Loss aversion

blocks.question: "Join 5000 marketers who already cut their reporting time in half"

feedbackCorrect.text: This line quantifies what the reader is actively losing — time, compounding weekly. Loss aversion works by making the cost of inaction feel concrete and painful. The reader isn't being offered something new; they're being shown what's already slipping away.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Urgency and scarcity create time pressure around a decision — "limited spots," "offer ends Friday." This line is not about the missing deadline, but about an ongoing loss the reader is experiencing right now, which is loss aversion: the pain of losing something outweighs the appeal of gaining something.

blocks.instruction: Which principle is being used in this copy line?

options.label: Loss aversion
Urgency and scarcity

blocks.question: "You're losing 6 hours a week to manual reporting. That's 300+ hours a year you'll never get back."

feedbackCorrect.text: A deadline ("closes Friday") and a limited quantity ("12 seats") create urgency and scarcity. This combination accelerates decisions by making the reader feel they might miss out if they wait.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Social proof would reference how many people have already enrolled, building trust through numbers. This line focuses on how few spots are left and when access disappears — that's urgency and scarcity, designed to compress the decision timeline.

blocks.instruction: Which principle is being used in this copy line?

options.label: Urgency and scarcity
Social proof

blocks.question: "Enrollment closes Friday — 12 seats remaining."

blocks.exampleResponse: Every month you delay switching, you're paying for a tool your team has already outgrown. The workarounds cost more than the migration ever would. 200 SaaS companies made the switch last quarter — most were live in under a week. See what migration looks like for your team.
blocks.prompt: Embed a specific psychology principle into your prompt to make the copy emotionally targeted.
blocks.template: Write [format] for [product] targeting [audience]. Use [psychology principle] as the primary emotional driver. The reader's main fear is disruption during the switch. Add CTA.

blocks.text: See how loss aversion shapes the entire tone — the copy leads with what the reader is already losing, not what they could gain. The psychology principle gave AI a clear emotional direction to write from. Different principles produce fundamentally different copy for the same product.
CTAs That Work

The final element is the CTA — the moment you ask the reader to act. The key to effective CTAs is matching the ask to the reader's awareness stage. Not every reader is in the same place in your funnel — some are just learning about you, others are comparing options, and some are ready to buy.

• Cold audience: top of the funnel, not ready to buy, need a low-commitment next step (e.g., "See how it works," "Read the case study")
  • Warm audience: middle of the funnel, comparing options and considering your solution, need a medium-commitment next step (e.g., "Start your free trial," "Book a 15-minute demo")
  • Hot audience: bottom of the funnel, ready to act and choose a solution, need a high-commitment next step with urgency or specificity (e.g., "Get started today," "Claim your spot — 12 left")

blocks.exampleResponse: Cold: "See a 2-minute demo" / "How it works" / "Browse customer stories" Warm: "Try free for 14 days" / "Book a walkthrough" / "Compare plans" Hot: "Start now — setup takes 5 minutes" / "Lock in this year's pricing" / "Join 3000+ teams today"
blocks.prompt: Use Copy.ai to quickly generate CTA variations for different awareness levels.
blocks.template: Generate [number] CTA variations for [product] at each funnel stage. Cold audience: low commitment. Warm audience: medium commitment. Hot audience: high commitment and urgency. Keep each CTA [length].

blocks.text: Great Work!

Notice how the commitment level scales with the funnel stage. A cold reader sees "browse customer stories" — zero risk. A hot reader sees "lock in this year's pricing" — urgency and a direct action. Matching the CTA to the reader's readiness is what makes it convert.

Before writing any copy, define these three foundations:
  • One-sentence offer: Who it's for, what it does, what outcome it delivers.
  • Message triangle: Offer + Outcome + Proof. If any element is missing, the copy won't convince.
  • Audience persona: Their frustration, desire, objection, and the language they use.
Then choose the psychology principle and CTA stage that match your reader's emotional state. This preparation feeds directly into every brief you write.

blocks.text: Know Before You Write

Imagine prompting AI to write a product page — and getting back copy so generic it could belong to any brand. The problem is starting to draft before you clearly know what to say.

In this lesson, you'll learn the strategic work that comes before drafting: defining a clear offer, researching your audience with AI, applying psychology principles, and writing CTAs that match every stage of the funnel.

feedbackCorrect.text: These three elements — audience, offer, and proof — form the foundation of every piece of effective copy. Without them, even a great framework like AIDA has nothing meaningful to work with. Tools, tone, and style come after the strategic groundwork.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Tools and tone matter, but they're execution decisions — they come after you know what to say. The most common issue in AI copywriting is drafting too soon, before you clarify who it's for, what you're offering, and why it matters. Strategy first, writing second.

blocks.text: The Three Foundations of Effective Copy
Every piece of persuasive copy rests on three elements:

• A clear offer: What are you selling and to whom?
  • A defined audience: Who are you writing for, and what do they care about?
  • A credible proof: Why should anyone believe your promise?
Let's explore each of them!
Start With a One-Sentence Offer

Before you open any AI tool, you need to answer one question: What exactly are you offering? A one-sentence offer defines the product, the audience, and the core outcome in a single, clear statement. If you can't say it in one sentence, your copy will be unfocused — and so will every AI prompt you write from it.
Compare these two:

• Vague: "We help businesses grow with our platform."
  • Clear: "We help e-commerce brands recover abandoned carts with automated email sequences that average 12% conversion."
The second version tells you who it's for, what it does, and what result to expect. That's a one-sentence offer.

correctTokens: a meal planning app called Mealwise
weekly meal planning taking too long
blocks.exampleResponse: Mealwise is a weekly meal-planning app that gives busy parents a personalized grocery list and 30-minute dinner recipes tailored to their family's dietary needs — cutting weekly food planning from 2 hours to 10 minutes.
blocks.prompt: Use Claude to sharpen a vague product idea into a focused one-sentence offer.
blocks.template: My product is [product]. It's for [audience] who struggle with [core problem]. Help me write a one-sentence offer that clearly states who it's for, what it does, and what specific outcome it delivers.
tokens: a meal planning app called Mealwise
weekly meal planning taking too long

blocks.text: Great!

Notice how much work that single sentence does: it names the audience, the product, the mechanism, and a measurable outcome. Every piece of copy you write for this product can now point back to this sentence for direction.
The Message Triangle
A one-sentence offer gets you started. To build copy that convinces, you need three elements working together — what we call the message triangle.

• Offer: What are you selling and to whom?
  • Outcome: What specific result does the reader get?
  • Proof: Why should they believe you?
Every strong piece of copy answers all three questions. Weak copy is almost always missing one.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! The offer is there (AI writing tool), and the outcome is stated (10x faster). The missing piece is proof — what makes "10x faster" credible? A stat, a case study, a specific mechanism. Without proof, bold claims feel like marketing noise.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The offer is present — "AI writing tool" tells you what the product is. "10x faster" is an outcome — it tells the reader what they'll get. The problem isn't that the outcome is weak; it's that there's no evidence to back it up. Speed is a clear benefit, but without evidence (a user study, a comparison, a concrete mechanism), the reader has no reason to believe it. Proof is what turns a promise into a persuasive claim.

options.label: Proof — there's no reason to believe the "10x faster" claim
Outcome — "10x faster" isn't specific enough to count as a real outcome
Offer — it doesn't say what the product costs

blocks.question: "Our AI writing tool helps you create content 10x faster." Which element of the message triangle is missing?

blocks.text: Types of Proof
Proof doesn't always mean testimonials or case studies. There are several types you can use depending on what's available:

• Social proof: user numbers, reviews
  • Process proof: explaining how or why something works
  • Specificity proof: concrete details that signal credibility ("847 teams" feels more real than "hundreds of teams")
  • Constraint proof: what you don't do ("We only work with B2B SaaS" signals expertise)
The more specific the proof, the stronger the trust.

correctTokens: a sleep coaching app called NightOwl
blocks.exampleResponse:
Offer: NightOwl is a sleep coaching app that builds personalized wind-down routines for adults who can't fall asleep without screens. Outcome: Users fall asleep 25 minutes faster within the first two weeks, without medication. Proof:
  1. Specificity: "Built on 12 peer-reviewed sleep studies."
  2. Social: "Used by 15,000 people in the last 6 months."
  3. Process: "The app adapts your routine nightly based on your sleep data."
blocks.prompt: Use Claude to build a complete message triangle for a product — offer, outcome, and proof.
blocks.template: Build a message triangle for [product]. Define the offer in one sentence. State the primary outcome for [audience]. Then suggest [number] types of [evidence] that would make the promise credible.
tokens: a sleep coaching app called NightOwl

blocks.text: Excellent!

You now have a repeatable structure for preparing any piece of copy. Define the offer, state the outcome, then choose the proof that makes it believable. This triangle will feed directly into every brief you write going forward.
Audience Research With AI

Your message triangle answers what you're saying. Audience research answers who you're saying it to — and how to say it in a way that resonates. AI can accelerate research dramatically. Instead of spending time reading reviews and forums, you can prompt AI to surface pain points, desires, objections, and language patterns.
Pain Points and Desires
Strong copy connects these two things:

• Pain points — the specific frustrations, problems, and obstacles your audience faces right now.
  • Desires — the outcomes and the future state your audience is trying to reach.
Building Audience Personas

The next step after recognizing pain points and desires is organizing that knowledge into a profile you can write to. An audience persona is a detailed profile of your ideal reader that goes beyond demographics. Personas give you a specific person to write to, which is why you'll produce sharper, more emotionally relevant copy.

blocks.exampleResponse: Name: Sarah, 34, marketing manager. Frustration: Spends Sunday evenings dreading the inbox she didn't clear on Friday. Tried: Todoist, sticky notes, blocking time on the calendar — none stuck. Secretly wants: To feel in control without thinking about productivity. Main objection: "Another app won't fix my habits." Her words: "I don't need more tools, I need fewer things on my plate."
blocks.prompt: Use ChatGPT to create a detailed audience persona based on a target market.
blocks.template: I'm writing copy for [product] targeting [audience]. Create a detailed persona including: their biggest frustration, what they've already tried, what they secretly want, their main objection to buying, and the exact language they'd use to describe their problem.

blocks.text: Notice the last section — "her words." That's the most valuable part. When your copy uses the same language your audience uses to describe their problem, it feels like you're reading their mind. AI can quickly surface this language, and you can validate it against real reviews and forums.

You can dive deeper into the audience language research. Use ChatGPT: paste in actual reviews or forum quotes and ask it to find patterns — the words and phrases that repeat across multiple people. When your copy mirrors that language, it creates instant recognition: "This is exactly my problem."
Audience Psychology in Your Prompts

Understanding your audience goes beyond demographics. Psychology principles help you tap into the emotional drivers behind decisions — and you can embed these principles directly into your AI prompts.
These three principles show up in effective copy because they tap into fundamental human decision-making patterns:

• Loss aversion hits hardest when your audience is already experiencing a cost. Lead with what they're losing.
  • Social proof works best when your audience feels uncertain or is comparing options. Numbers and peer validation reduce perceived risk.
  • Urgency and scarcity accelerate decisions when the reader is already interested. A deadline or limited quantity pushes them past hesitation.
The key is choosing the principle that matches where your reader is emotionally, not stacking all three at once.

The Structure Behind Persuasion

You know how to transform abstract product ideas into focused offers, detailed personas, and psychology-driven prompts. Now it's time to turn that preparation into structured, persuasive copy. In this lesson, you'll learn AIDA — the most widely used persuasive framework in copywriting — and run the full brief → draft → critique → rewrite loop on a real draft. Let's get started!

feedbackCorrect.text: Persuasive copy is structured intentionally — it moves the reader step by step from awareness to action. Emotional language and long benefit lists can actually weaken copy if they're not organized around a clear path to one decision.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Stacking adjectives or listing every benefit often overwhelms the reader instead of persuading them. Persuasion works through structure — guiding the reader from their problem to your solution to a clear next step. Without that structure, even great language falls flat.

blocks.instruction: Select all possible answers

options.label: It presents as many benefits as possible, so the reader sees the full value
It follows a deliberate structure that builds toward a specific action
It uses powerful adjectives and emotional language throughout
It connects the reader's problem to a clear outcome before asking them to act

blocks.question: What do you think makes copy persuasive rather than just informative?

blocks.text: The AIDA Framework

AIDA is one of the oldest and most widely used persuasive frameworks in copywriting. It gives your copy a clear four-stage structure that mirrors how people make decisions — from noticing something to taking action.
Let's see what each stage does:

• Attention: Stop the reader. A hook, a bold claim, a question that hits a nerve.
  • Interest: Hold them. Share relevant details, specifics, or a story that connects to their situation.
  • Desire: Make them want it. Show the outcome, paint the transformation, make it feel real.
  • Action: Tell them what to do. A clear, specific CTA with no ambiguity.
Every stage has one job. Skip one, and the whole sequence breaks.

blocks.exampleResponse: Ready to get fit? Our app has everything you need to reach your goals. With expert workouts and personalized plans, you'll see results fast. Whether you're a beginner or advanced, we've got you covered. Download now and start your journey to a healthier you!
blocks.prompt: Try generating AIDA copy with a minimal prompt.
blocks.template: Write an AIDA [format] for my [product]

feedbackCorrect.text: The structure is technically there, but none of it is specific. "Ready to get fit?" could be the opening line of any fitness ad ever written. "See results fast" says nothing concrete. AIDA without specificity is just a template filled with filler. The framework only works when each stage earns the reader's attention with real details.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Following the AIDA structure isn't enough on its own. Each stage needs to do specific work — a hook that's relevant to this audience, details about this product, outcomes that feel real. A stronger hook alone won't fix the vague interest, desire, and action sections. The whole draft needs more direction from the brief.

options.label: Yes, it follows the AIDA structure and ends with a clear CTA
It's close — just needs a stronger opening hook to grab attention
No, every stage is generic and could apply to any fitness product

blocks.question: Does this AIDA email work?

correctTokens: busy professionals with no gym time
blocks.exampleResponse: You have 20 minutes between meetings. That's enough. FitSpark gives you trainer-built HIIT sessions for small spaces — no equipment, no commute. In 4 weeks, users report more energy by 5 p.m., instead of crashing after lunch. Try it free for 14 days.
blocks.prompt: Now give AI the context it needs. Define the audience, product, and what each AIDA stage should focus on.
blocks.template: Write an AIDA email for [product] targeting [audience]. Attention: hook with [hook approach]. Interest: mention its fit for small spaces. Desire: emphasize energy and daily performance. CTA: [action].
tokens: busy professionals with no gym time

feedbackCorrect.text: When each AIDA stage has a defined focus — a specific hook, a concrete detail, a real outcome — AI writes with precision. The framework becomes a set of constraints, not just a label. That's what turned generic filler into copy with a clear path from attention to action.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Tool choice and prompt length help, but the improvement came from giving each AIDA stage a specific job. "Hook with their time constraints" is a different instruction than just "get attention." Specificity within the framework drives quality, regardless of which tool you use or how long the prompt is.

options.label: The second prompt was more detailed, and longer prompts always produce better copy
Claude is better than ChatGPT at writing AIDA emails
Each AIDA stage had a specific focus, so AI wrote with the direction and not filler

blocks.question: Why did this draft outperform the first one?

blocks.text: Great Work!
You've drafted a solid AIDA email. But in a real project, the first draft is rarely the final one. Now it's time to practice the full brief → draft → critique → rewrite loop on this very draft.
The Critique Step

You have a draft. Before rewriting anything, you need to diagnose what's working and what's not. The critique step means evaluating your draft against clear criteria — not just rereading it and hoping something jumps out.

feedbackCorrect.text: The Attention hook is specific and relevant, the Interest section includes concrete details, and the CTA is clear. The Desire stage is the weakest link — "more energy by 5 p.m." states a benefit, but doesn't make the reader feel the change. That's the one lever worth rewriting.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The Attention hook works because it mirrors the reader's reality, not because it's dramatic. The CTA is simple by design — clarity beats cleverness. The real gap lies in Desire: it states a fact rather than painting a picture. When you critique, look for the stage that does its job least vividly.

options.label: Desire. "More energy by 5 p.m." is decent, but doesn't create a vivid, emotional picture
Attention. "You have 20 minutes between meetings" isn't dramatic enough
Action. "Try it free for 14 days" is too simple to be effective

blocks.question: Look at the FitSpark AIDA email. Which stage is the weakest?

blocks.text: The Rewrite Step

You've identified the weakness: the Desire section doesn't create a vivid enough picture. Now, instead of rewriting the whole email, give AI a targeted instruction — fix this one section with a specific direction for improvement.

blocks.exampleResponse: Four weeks in, FitSpark users say the same thing: they stopped hitting snooze, stopped canceling evening plans, and stopped dreading the afternoon crash. That's not hype — that's what happens when your workout actually fits your day.
blocks.prompt: Rewrite only the Desire section of the FitSpark email. Give Claude specific direction on how to make it more emotionally vivid.
blocks.template: The Desire section of this AIDA email is weak: "In 4 weeks, users report more energy by 5 p.m. instead of crashing after lunch." Rewrite only this section for [product] targeting [audience]. Make the outcome feel [quality]. Keep it under [length].

blocks.text: Excellent!

You didn't start over. You identified the single weakest element, gave AI a precise rewrite instruction, and the copy got measurably stronger. That's the loop in action — and it works the same way whether you're writing emails, ads, or landing pages.

The AIDA framework provides the structure for your copy. The brief → draft → critique → rewrite loop gives you a system to improve it.
  • Brief: Define what each AIDA stage should focus on.
  • Draft: Generate the full AIDA sequence with AI.
  • Critique: Evaluate each stage: which one is the weakest?
  • Rewrite: Fix that one stage with a targeted instruction.
Each loop makes the copy sharper.
blocks.title: AIDA + The Loop

blocks.text: Writing Clear, Concise Copy
A solid AIDA structure won't save your copy if the writing itself is vague or bloated. The next skill is learning to cut the fluff. There's a simple test that makes this instant.
The "So What?" Test

After every claim in your copy, ask, "So what? Why should the reader care?" If you can't answer immediately with a specific outcome or proof, the sentence is filler and needs to be rewritten or cut. This test catches the vague, impressive-sounding phrases that feel like good copy but say nothing.

pairs.left: "We use cutting-edge AI technology"
pairs.right: What specific result does the technology create for the reader?

pairs.left: "Our team brings 20 years of experience"
pairs.right: What did those years teach them that helps the reader?

pairs.left: "We're passionate about delivering quality"
pairs.right: What does "quality" mean in concrete terms?

blocks.prompt: Each copy line fails the "So What?" test. Match it to the question that exposes what's missing.
blocks.title: Applying the "So What?" Test

blocks.text: Each line sounds professional but says nothing. The "So What?" test forces you to replace vague claims with specific outcomes. AI can do this for you when you give it the right instructions.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Sentence 1 fails: "innovative technology" and "premium solutions" say nothing specific. 
Fix: "Our inventory system cuts stockouts by 30% using real-time demand forecasting." 

Sentence 2 fails: "excellence in everything" is vague. 
Fix: "Every client gets a dedicated account manager who responds within 2 hours."
blocks.prompt: Use AI to evaluate a copy block and rewrite the sentences that fail the test.
blocks.template: Here's a product description: "We leverage innovative technology to deliver premium solutions for modern businesses. Our dedicated team ensures excellence in everything we do." Apply the [test type] to each sentence. For sentences that fail, rewrite them to include [validation signals].

blocks.text: Great Work!
Notice how the rewrite replaced vague claims with concrete details the reader can evaluate. That's the "So What?" test at work. It applies to every format you'll write in this course.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! This option puts the actor first and adds a specific time detail — "in seconds." It's more direct, more energetic, and gives the reader something concrete. Active voice is almost always stronger in copy because it keeps the reader moving forward.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. This option communicates the same idea but buries the actor ("our AI assistant") at the end and lacks specificity. In copy, you want the reader to know who does what immediately. Active voice keeps sentences lean and forward-moving.

options.label: "Your workflow is streamlined by our AI assistant"
"Our AI assistant streamlines your workflow in seconds"

blocks.question: Which version of copy do you think would work better on a product page?

blocks.text: The Power of an Active Voice
There's one more technique that instantly sharpens copy: active voice. In the active voice, the subject does the action.
Compare:

• Passive: "Your data is protected by 256-bit encryption."
  • Active: "256-bit encryption protects your data."
Active voice is shorter, more direct, and creates more energy. Passive voice buries the actor and slows the reader.

blocks.exampleResponse:
1. "Our AI platform delivers results."
  2. "A dedicated specialist reviews your account."
  3. "We add new features every month."
Each rewrite puts the actor first — shorter, sharper, and the reader immediately knows who's doing what.
blocks.prompt: Use AI to quickly convert passive copy lines into active, direct versions.
blocks.template:
Rewrite these [number] copy lines in [voice type] to make them [style]
  1. "Results are delivered by our AI-powered platform."
  2. "Your account will be reviewed by a dedicated specialist."
  3. "New features are added to the product every month."

blocks.text: Structure, Clarity, and Voice

You've now practiced the AIDA framework from draft to targeted rewrite, learned the "So What?" test for cutting vague filler, and used active voice to make every sentence more direct. 

These three techniques — structure, clarity, and voice — work together across every format you'll write in this course.

• AIDA gives copy a persuasive structure: Attention → Interest → Desire → Action. Each stage needs a specific focus.
  • The loop (brief → draft → critique → rewrite) improves copy one lever at a time instead of starting over.
  • The "So What?" test catches vague claims — if a sentence doesn't point to a specific outcome or proof, cut or rewrite it.
  • Active voice puts the actor first, making copy shorter, clearer, and more direct.

Edit Like a Professional

You have an AI-generated draft, and it doesn't feel right. You reread it three times, change a few words, and hope the next version lands better. But such editing is not strategic nor systematic.  

In this lesson, you'll learn how to critique copy using a clear rubric, improve drafts, translate client feedback into precise rewrite instructions, and build a repeatable editing workflow.

feedbackCorrect.text: Effective critique is specific and prioritized. Evaluating against defined criteria tells you exactly what's weak, and focusing on the single biggest issue prevents scattered rewrites that change everything without improving anything.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Rereading without criteria leads to vague feelings instead of an actionable diagnosis. Asking AI to "make it better" gives it no direction. And grammar is the last thing to check — structural issues like a weak offer or missing proof have far more impact on whether the copy actually works.

blocks.question: What makes reviewing an AI-generated draft effective?

blocks.text: Why Editing Fails

The most common editing mistake is trying to fix everything at once. You read a draft, feel like something's off, and either rewrite the whole thing or give AI a vague instruction like "make it punchier." The result? Another draft that's not necessarily better — just different. Professional editing is the opposite. It's diagnosis first, then targeted surgery.
The Copy Rubric
A rubric gives you a repeatable set of criteria to evaluate any piece of copy — no guesswork, no gut feelings. Instead of asking "Is this good?", you ask specific questions about each element.
Here are the criteria that apply across formats:

• Clarity: Can the reader understand the core message in one read?
  • Specificity: Are claims backed by concrete details?
  • Offer strength: Is it clear what the reader gets and why it matters?
  • Proof: Is there a reason to believe the promise?
  • Structure: Does the copy flow logically toward the CTA?
  • CTA: Is the action clear, specific, and matched to the reader's stage?
Each criterion is a lens. You evaluate the draft through one lens at a time.

blocks.exampleResponse: Clarity — weak. "Helps teams work better" doesn't say what the product does. Specificity — weak. "Powerful features," "results fast," and "intuitive" are vague. Offer strength — weak. No clear outcome or value proposition. Proof — adequate. "Thousands of companies" provides some social proof but lacks specificity. Structure — adequate. Follows a logical order, but each section is too thin. CTA — weak. "Get started today" doesn't say what happens next or why now.
blocks.prompt: Use Claude to critique a draft against the rubric.
blocks.template:
This is a landing page draft:
"Our platform helps teams work better. With powerful features and an intuitive interface, you'll see results fast. Thousands of companies trust us. Get started today."
Evaluate this draft against these [number] criteria: [criterion], specificity, offer strength, proof, structure, CTA. For each one, rate it as strong, adequate, or weak, and explain why in one sentence.

blocks.text: Great Work!

Look at what the rubric reveals: four out of 6 elements are weak. Without the rubric, you might have just felt "this doesn't sound great" and asked AI to rewrite everything. With the rubric, you know exactly where the problems are — and you can fix them in order of impact.
One Lever Per Pass

You've diagnosed the weaknesses. Now the key principle: change one lever per pass. Fix the offer strength first. Then reassess. Then fix specificity. Then reassess again. Why? Because when you change everything at once, you can't tell what improved the copy and what made it worse. One change per pass keeps every improvement measurable and intentional.

feedbackCorrect.text: Clarity is always the first lever. If the reader doesn't understand what you're offering, a better CTA or more specific details won't help — they've already lost interest. Fix the foundation, then build up from there.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A strong CTA matters, but it can't save copy that's unclear. Fixing everything at once produces unfocused rewrites. Start with clarity — it's the foundation. Once the core message is clear, improving specificity and the CTA becomes much easier because the direction is set.

options.label: All three at once — fixing them separately takes too long for a real project
CTA — it's the last thing the reader sees, so it has the most direct impact on conversion
Clarity — if the reader can't understand the core message, nothing else matters

When iterating on a draft:
  • Diagnose using the rubric: Rate each criterion.
  • Prioritize: Pick the single weakest element.

• "This doesn't feel right."
  • "Can we make it more engaging?"
  • "I don't love the tone."
  • "It needs more punch."
None of these tells you what to change. Your job is to translate the feedback into a specific rubric criterion and a clear rewrite direction.

blocks.question: Why do you think headlines deserve special attention in the copywriting process?

blocks.text: Headlines sit at the intersection of reader attention and search visibility. That's why writing them well requires understanding both. Let's start with the search side — the SEO fundamentals every copywriter needs to know.
SEO Fundamentals for Copywriters

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) is about making your copy visible to people who are actively searching for what you offer. For copywriters, you don't need to become a technical SEO expert. 

You just need to understand three things:

• Search intent
  • Keywords
  • The balance between writing for humans and search engines
Search Intent

Search intent is the reason behind a search query — what the person wants when they type something into Google. This is the most important concept for SEO copywriting, because if your headline and page don't match the searcher's intent, they'll click away immediately — and search engines will notice.
There are four main types of search intent:

• Informational: The searcher wants to learn something (e.g., "how to write email subject lines").
  • Commercial: The searcher is researching options before buying (e.g., "best email marketing tools").
  • Transactional: The searcher is ready to act (e.g., "Mailchimp pricing plans").
  • Navigational: The searcher is looking for a specific page (e.g., "Mailchimp login").
As a copywriter, you'll mostly write for informational, commercial, and transactional intent. Each one requires a different headline approach.

feedbackCorrect.text: The searcher is comparing options — "best" signals they're evaluating, not ready to buy yet. Commercial intent means they want helpful comparisons, reviews, or rankings to narrow their choice. Your headline should promise clarity and comparison, not a hard sell.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Transactional intent means the searcher is ready to act right now — "buy," "pricing," "sign up." This query uses "best," which signals they're still researching and comparing. That's commercial intent, and the headline needs to match their evaluation mindset.

blocks.text: Keywords

The next step is the keywords. A keyword is the word or phrase someone types into a search engine. Your job as a copywriter is to identify the keywords your audience uses, then weave them naturally into your headlines and copy.

Attention to "naturally". Stuffing keywords into awkward sentences hurts readability and can actually damage your search rankings. Modern SEO rewards copy that reads well to humans while including relevant terms.
Using Semrush's Keyword Magic Tool

Let's find real keywords to write for. Meet Semrush's Keyword Magic Tool that helps you turn one topic into a big list of related keyword ideas, so you can quickly find what people search for. It also shows helpful metrics such as search volume, difficulty, and intent type.
Keyword Research Workflow
Let's see how to find your target keyword in the Keyword Magic Tool:

1. Enter a broad seed keyword related to your topic (e.g., "project management software").
  2. Filter by intent: select Commercial if you're writing a comparison page, Informational for a how-to guide, or Transactional for a product page.
  3. Sort by keyword difficulty to find terms you can realistically rank for.
  4. Pick a keyword with reasonable search volume that matches your page goal.
Great!

Notice how the Intent column guided the keyword choice. If you'd picked an informational keyword like "what is project management" for a comparison page, the content wouldn't match what the searcher is looking for, and they'd bounce. Intent alignment is the foundation of SEO copywriting.
Headline Formulas
With your keyword and intent locked in, it's time to write headlines. Proven headline formulas give you a reliable starting structure, and AI can generate dozens of variations from each one.
Here are four formulas that consistently perform across formats:

• How-To: How to achieve an outcome without a common objection — works for informational intent (e.g., "How to Improve Email Open Rates Without Growing Your List")
  • Listicle: Number of things that deliver results — works for informational and commercial intent. (e.g., "9 Email Marketing Tools That Actually Save You Time”)

• Direct Benefit: Specific outcome for a specific audience — works for commercial and transactional intent. (e.g., "Faster Campaign Reporting for In-House Marketing Teams”)
  • Question: A Pain point question and a specific promise — works across all intent types. (e.g., "Tired of Low Open Rates? Here's What Top Marketers Do Differently”)
Each formula serves a different intent. Matching the formula to the intent gives your headline the best chance of ranking and clicking.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Commercial intent means the searcher is comparing options. A listicle with a number and comparison angle directly matches that mindset — they want a ranked or organized overview of their choices. The How-To formula better aligns with informational intent, and the Question formula doesn't signal comparison clearly enough.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. The How-To and Question formulas are strong, but they don't align with commercial intent as precisely. The searcher wants to compare tools, not learn a process or be asked about their pain points. A listicle headline promises the organized comparison they're looking for — and that alignment is what drives both clicks and rankings.

Writing for Humans and Search Engines
A common trap in SEO copywriting is writing headlines that rank well but read awkwardly, or headlines that sound great but miss the keyword entirely. The best SEO headlines do both.
Here are three rules for balancing search and readability:

• Lead with the keyword when possible: "Best Project Management Tools..." is stronger than "Here Are Some Tools for Project Management..."
  • Aim for 50-60 characters: Titles longer than roughly 60 characters often get truncated in Google search results. Keeping your headline within 50-60 characters ensures it is fully visible.
  • Write for the click, not just the rank: A headline that ranks high, but nobody clicks is still failing. The headline needs to promise something specific enough to earn the click.

B2B Headlines — What Changes
Everything you've learned applies to B2B headlines too: keyword research, intent matching, and proven formulas still work. The differences are in tone, specificity, and what the reader values.

B2B readers are typically evaluating solutions for their team or company, not for themselves personally. They care about ROI, efficiency, risk reduction, and how to justify the decision to stakeholders.
This changes the headline approach:

• B2C: "7 Best Meal Kit Deliveries for Busy Parents"
  • B2B: "7 Best Project Management Tools for Enterprise Teams (Ranked by ROI and Scalability)"
B2B headlines often include qualifiers like company size, industry, or business outcome. The formulas stay the same — the specifics inside them shift toward professional decision-making.

blocks.question: Why do you think headlines deserve special attention in the copywriting process?

blocks.text: Headlines sit at the intersection of reader attention and search visibility. That's why writing them well requires understanding both. Let's start with the search side — the SEO fundamentals every copywriter needs to know.
SEO Fundamentals for Copywriters

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) is about making your copy visible to people who are actively searching for what you offer. For copywriters, you don't need to become a technical SEO expert. 

You just need to understand three things:

• Search intent
  • Keywords
  • The balance between writing for humans and search engines
Search Intent

Search intent is the reason behind a search query — what the person wants when they type something into Google. This is the most important concept for SEO copywriting, because if your headline and page don't match the searcher's intent, they'll click away immediately — and search engines will notice.
There are four main types of search intent:

• Informational: The searcher wants to learn something (e.g., "how to write email subject lines").
  • Commercial: The searcher is researching options before buying (e.g., "best email marketing tools").
  • Transactional: The searcher is ready to act (e.g., "Mailchimp pricing plans").
  • Navigational: The searcher is looking for a specific page (e.g., "Mailchimp login").
As a copywriter, you'll mostly write for informational, commercial, and transactional intent. Each one requires a different headline approach.

feedbackCorrect.text: The searcher is comparing options — "best" signals they're evaluating, not ready to buy yet. Commercial intent means they want helpful comparisons, reviews, or rankings to narrow their choice. Your headline should promise clarity and comparison, not a hard sell.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Transactional intent means the searcher is ready to act right now — "buy," "pricing," "sign up." This query uses "best," which signals they're still researching and comparing. That's commercial intent, and the headline needs to match their evaluation mindset.

blocks.instruction: What type of search intent does this query have?

options.label: Commercial
Transactional

blocks.question: "Best CRM software for small businesses"

feedbackCorrect.text: "How to" is a classic informational signal — the searcher wants to learn a skill or solve a problem, not buy a product. Your headline should promise actionable knowledge, not a product comparison.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Commercial intent involves comparing products or services. This query starts with "how to," which means the searcher wants education, not a buying guide. Informational headlines should promise useful, specific knowledge.

blocks.instruction: What type of search intent does this query have?

options.label: Informational
Commercial

blocks.question: "How to improve email open rates"

feedbackCorrect.text: The searcher already knows the product and is looking for pricing details — they're close to a purchase decision. Transactional intent means the headline should be direct and specific: no educational hooks, just clear information that helps them act.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Informational queries seek knowledge or how-to guidance. This searcher already knows what they want (Semrush) and is looking for pricing to make a buying decision. That's transactional — the headline should deliver the specific information they need to commit.

options.label: Transactional
Informational

blocks.question: "Semrush pricing monthly plan"

blocks.text: Keywords

The next step is the keywords. A keyword is the word or phrase someone types into a search engine. Your job as a copywriter is to identify the keywords your audience uses, then weave them naturally into your headlines and copy.

Attention to "naturally". Stuffing keywords into awkward sentences hurts readability and can actually damage your search rankings. Modern SEO rewards copy that reads well to humans while including relevant terms.
Using Semrush's Keyword Magic Tool

Let's find real keywords to write for. Meet Semrush's Keyword Magic Tool that helps you turn one topic into a big list of related keyword ideas, so you can quickly find what people search for. It also shows helpful metrics such as search volume, difficulty, and intent type.
Keyword Research Workflow
Let's see how to find your target keyword in the Keyword Magic Tool:

1. Enter a broad seed keyword related to your topic (e.g., "project management software").
  2. Filter by intent: select Commercial if you're writing a comparison page, Informational for a how-to guide, or Transactional for a product page.
  3. Sort by keyword difficulty to find terms you can realistically rank for.
  4. Pick a keyword with reasonable search volume that matches your page goal.
Great!

Notice how the Intent column guided the keyword choice. If you'd picked an informational keyword like "what is project management" for a comparison page, the content wouldn't match what the searcher is looking for, and they'd bounce. Intent alignment is the foundation of SEO copywriting.
Headline Formulas
With your keyword and intent locked in, it's time to write headlines. Proven headline formulas give you a reliable starting structure, and AI can generate dozens of variations from each one.
Here are four formulas that consistently perform across formats:

• How-To: How to achieve an outcome without a common objection — works for informational intent (e.g., "How to Improve Email Open Rates Without Growing Your List")
  • Listicle: Number of things that deliver results — works for informational and commercial intent. (e.g., "9 Email Marketing Tools That Actually Save You Time”)

• Direct Benefit: Specific outcome for a specific audience — works for commercial and transactional intent. (e.g., "Faster Campaign Reporting for In-House Marketing Teams”)
  • Question: A Pain point question and a specific promise — works across all intent types. (e.g., "Tired of Low Open Rates? Here's What Top Marketers Do Differently”)
Each formula serves a different intent. Matching the formula to the intent gives your headline the best chance of ranking and clicking.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Commercial intent means the searcher is comparing options. A listicle with a number and comparison angle directly matches that mindset — they want a ranked or organized overview of their choices. The How-To formula better aligns with informational intent, and the Question formula doesn't signal comparison clearly enough.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. The How-To and Question formulas are strong, but they don't align with commercial intent as precisely. The searcher wants to compare tools, not learn a process or be asked about their pain points. A listicle headline promises the organized comparison they're looking for — and that alignment is what drives both clicks and rankings.

options.label: Listicle — "7 Best Email Marketing Tools (Compared by Features and Price)"
Question — "Struggling With Email Marketing? Here's What Top Marketers Use"
How-To — "How to Choose the Right Email Marketing Tool"

blocks.text: Excellent!

Seven variations, each using a different formula, all including the keyword naturally, and all aligned with commercial intent. This is how AI accelerates headline writing: you provide the strategic direction, and AI produces the volume for testing.
Writing for Humans and Search Engines
A common trap in SEO copywriting is writing headlines that rank well but read awkwardly, or headlines that sound great but miss the keyword entirely. The best SEO headlines do both.
Here are three rules for balancing search and readability:

• Lead with the keyword when possible: "Best Project Management Tools..." is stronger than "Here Are Some Tools for Project Management..."
  • Aim for 50-60 characters: Titles longer than roughly 60 characters often get truncated in Google search results. Keeping your headline within 50-60 characters ensures it is fully visible.
  • Write for the click, not just the rank: A headline that ranks high, but nobody clicks is still failing. The headline needs to promise something specific enough to earn the click.

blocks.exampleResponse: "Best Project Management Tools for Small Teams: A Simple Guide to Choosing the Right One"

blocks.text: Great Work!
The keyword now leads the headline, it fits within the character limit, and it still reads naturally. That's the balance — search engines see relevance, readers see a clear promise.
B2B Headlines — What Changes
Everything you've learned applies to B2B headlines too: keyword research, intent matching, and proven formulas still work. The differences are in tone, specificity, and what the reader values.

B2B readers are typically evaluating solutions for their team or company, not for themselves personally. They care about ROI, efficiency, risk reduction, and how to justify the decision to stakeholders.
This changes the headline approach:

• B2C: "7 Best Meal Kit Deliveries for Busy Parents"
  • B2B: "7 Best Project Management Tools for Enterprise Teams (Ranked by ROI and Scalability)"
B2B headlines often include qualifiers like company size, industry, or business outcome. The formulas stay the same — the specifics inside them shift toward professional decision-making.

feedbackCorrect.text: "Sales teams" and "close deals" are business-specific outcomes. B2B headlines speak to professional roles and measurable business results. A B2C headline for CRM-adjacent products would focus on personal outcomes, such as "stay organized" or "never forget a follow-up."

feedbackIncorrect.text: The language here is business-focused — "sales teams" and "close deals" are professional contexts, not personal ones. B2C headlines target individual benefits and personal outcomes. This headline is built for a business buyer evaluating tools for their team.

feedbackIncorrect.text: This headline speaks directly to an individual consumer — personal purchase, personal use. B2B headlines would reference teams, business outcomes, or professional decision-making. "Tested and ranked" is a review format, but the audience is clearly a consumer.

  • SEO + copy balance is important. A headline needs to rank and compel a click.

Pages That Convert

A visitor clicks your headline. They land on the page — and stay there for quite a while, because both the headline and the landing page did their job. 

In this lesson, you'll learn how to create high-converting landing pages, write each section, make web copy scannable, and address objections before they stop the reader from acting.

feedbackCorrect.text: A landing page is defined by its focus — one goal, one action. Every section, from the hero to the final CTA, exists to move the reader toward that single decision. Trying to cover everything or appeal to multiple segments dilutes that focus and hurts conversions.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Cramming everything onto one page overwhelms the reader rather than guiding them. Targeting multiple segments splits the message, weakening its relevance. A homepage serves navigation across many goals — a landing page does the opposite: it eliminates distractions and channels all attention toward one decision.
