Building Your AI Copywriting Business

You've spent 11 lessons learning how to write major copywriting formats with AI — from headlines and landing pages to ads and long-form content. Let's turn those skills into income!

In this lesson, you'll learn how to build a portfolio, find and pitch your first clients, set rates that reflect the value, and navigate the ethics of AI-assisted copywriting.
Your Portfolio
A portfolio is what turns "I can write copy" into proof. Clients hire based on the work they can see. Your portfolio shows them what working with you looks like.

If you're a beginner, you can create spec work — sample projects for real or invented brands that demonstrate your skills. The exercises you've completed in this course are a starting point, but portfolio pieces need more polish and context.
Always label spec work clearly. Mark each piece as "Spec Project" or "Sample Work," so no one assumes a real brand hired or endorsed you.
blocks.title: A Note on Spec Work

feedbackCorrect.text: Clients care most about your thinking process — can you understand a business goal and translate it into copy that serves that goal? A visual mockup looks nice, but doesn't show strategy. Multiple drafts show process but not the "why" behind decisions.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Visual mockups demonstrate design awareness, and showing drafts proves you iterate — both have value. But neither answers the client's core question: "Does this person understand my business problem?" You need to demonstrate strategic thinking directly, which is what clients are paying for.

A landing page with three draft versions showing how the copy evolved
A landing page with the brief, the final copy, and a short explanation of the strategic choices behind it

blocks.question: Which portfolio piece demonstrates the most value to a potential client?

blocks.text: What Makes a Strong Portfolio Piece
A strong portfolio piece demonstrates thinking behind the copy. Clients want to see that you understand the strategy.
Every portfolio piece should include:

• Brief: What was the goal, audience, and key message?
  • Copy: The actual deliverable (landing page, email sequence, ad set, etc.).
  • Reasoning: Why you made the choices you did. Which framework did you use? Why that tone? Why that structure?
This format shows the client you're a strategic thinker.
Building Your First Portfolio

Start with 3-5 pieces that cover different formats. A strong starter portfolio might include a landing page, a 3-4 email welcome sequence, a set of ad variations, and a product page or a long-form article.

correctTokens: Mealwise (meal planning app for busy parents)
blocks.exampleResponse:
I structured this landing page around the AIDA framework because the audience needs to move from attention to action on a single page. 

The hero leads with the time-saving outcome ("meal planning in 10 minutes") because our audience's biggest frustration is planning. The objection-handling section addresses the #1 reason trial users churn: worry that their family won't eat the recipes. 

Every section is designed to reduce one barrier between "this looks interesting" and "start my free trial."

Write a short [length] "reasoning" section explaining my choices. Write it in first person, as if I'm presenting this to a potential client.

blocks.text: Finding Clients
With a portfolio ready to show, the next step is getting it in front of the right people. There are three main channels for finding copywriting clients, each with different effort-to-reward profiles.

Freelance platforms (Upwork, Fiverr, Contra) — lower rates but steady volume. Good for building experience and reviews. Competition is high, so your portfolio and proposal quality matter more than anywhere else.

Cold outreach — you contact businesses directly with a personalized pitch. Higher effort per lead, but higher rates and stronger relationships. Best for targeting specific industries or company sizes you want to work with.

Referrals and network — the highest-converting channel, but it takes time to build. Every client you do great work for becomes a potential source of future work. This is a long game, not a starting strategy.
Writing a Cold Pitch

Freelance platforms have built-in traffic, and referrals come from past work. Cold outreach requires you to earn attention from scratch.

Cold outreach only works when the pitch is specific to the business you're contacting. Generic pitches ("I'm a copywriter, let me know if you need help") get ignored. A strong cold pitch follows a simple structure.

1. Specific observation: Show you've looked at their business. Reference their website, a recent campaign, or a specific page.
  2. Identified opportunity: Name one thing that could be stronger — without insulting them.
  3. Your suggestion: Suggest a concrete step, not a vague promise.
  4. Low-friction CTA: Don't ask for a contract. Ask for a conversation.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Hi — I came across BrewBox's landing page while researching DTC coffee brands. The product photography is great, but I noticed the hero section leads with "Premium Single-Origin, Delivered Monthly," which describes the product but doesn't tell me why I'd switch from my current coffee routine.

A benefit-led headline like "Wake Up to Coffee You'll Actually Look Forward To" with a supporting line about the sourcing and freshness could give visitors a reason to stay on the page longer.

I put together a few ideas for how the full page could convert better. Want me to send them over?
blocks.prompt: Use Claude to draft a personalized cold outreach email.
blocks.template: I'm a freelance copywriter reaching out to [business type]. Draft a cold pitch email that opens with a specific observation about their page, identifies 1 improvement opportunity, suggests what I'd do differently, and ends with a low-commitment CTA. Tone: [tone].

blocks.text: Well Done!
The pitch works because it's specific — it references a real page, names a real issue, offers a real suggestion, and asks for a small next step.
Setting Your Rates

You can write a great pitch and land the client — let's talk about the prices. Pricing is one of the hardest decisions for new copywriters. The key principle: charge for the value of the output, not the time it took. A landing page that drives $50K in revenue is worth the same to the client whether it took you 2 hours or 20.
There are three common pricing models:

• Per-project: Fixed price for a defined deliverable (e.g., "$800 for a landing page"). Clients like the predictability. Best when the scope is clear.
  • Retainer: Monthly fee for ongoing work (e.g., "$2500/month for 8 emails + 12 social posts"). Provides stable income. Best for long-term relationships.
  • Per-word or per-hour: Common on freelance platforms, but often undervalues your work. You can use it as a starting point, but then move to a per-project basis as you build experience.

blocks.text: The Ethics of AI-Assisted Copywriting

Now for the most sensitive part every AI copywriter faces — ethics.

Using AI to write copy isn't cheating, but it does raise questions you need to think through. How you handle these questions defines whether clients trust you long-term.
Transparency

Should you tell clients you use AI? The answer is yes, when asked — and proactively when it's relevant. Many clients already expect AI involvement. What they care about is quality. Hiding AI use and getting caught damages trust far more than being upfront.
Ownership and Editing

AI generates raw material. You shape it with brief, framework choices, editing, and strategic thinking. The final deliverable reflects your expertise, not AI's. 

That said, never submit unedited AI output. Every piece should go through the full workflow: brief → draft → critique → rewrite.
Accuracy

AI can confidently state things that aren't true. Every claim, statistic, and brand detail in your copy must be verified. This is your responsibility. If an AI draft says "rated #1 by Consumer Reports," you confirm that before it goes to the client. The client is paying for copy they can publish — that means accuracy is non-negotiable.

feedbackCorrect.text: This answer is honest and positions AI as a professional tool. It acknowledges AI use while making clear that your strategic thinking, editing, and expertise drive the result. The second answer is dishonest. The third dramatically undersells your contribution.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Downplaying AI use risks losing the client's trust entirely. But overcorrecting by saying "AI wrote it" ignores the work you did: writing the brief, choosing the framework, and editing the output through multiple passes. Honesty builds long-term trust.

options.label: "Yes, I wrote every word myself. AI was just a spell-checker."
"I use AI as part of my writing process. The strategy, structure, and editing are mine."
"No, AI wrote it. I just edited a few sentences."

blocks.question: A client asks you to write a product page. You use Claude to draft it, then edit and refine the output. The client asks, "Did you write this yourself?" What's the best response?

blocks.text: Plagiarism and Originality

AI models are trained on existing text, which means outputs can occasionally echo existing copy. For anything client-facing, run final copy through a plagiarism checker (Grammarly, Copyscape, or Quetext) before delivery. This takes two minutes and protects both you and your client.

feedbackCorrect.text: The copy went through your full professional process — brief, AI draft, heavy rewrite, fact-checking. The final product reflects your judgment and skill.

feedbackIncorrect.text: AI drafts can contain errors, but that's exactly what the editing workflow catches. Thorough editing and fact-checking address the risks that come with any first draft — whether AI-generated or not.

feedbackCorrect.text: Speed matters, but not more than accuracy. Unedited AI output can contain false claims, awkward phrasing, or generic copy that doesn't match the brief. If the deadline is tight, it's better to send a strong draft with a note ("final version by noon") than to deliver unverified work that could damage the client's reputation — and yours.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Meeting deadlines is important, but delivering unverified copy with potential false claims creates a much bigger problem than a short delay. AI can hallucinate statistics, invent testimonials, or produce claims that don't hold up. A quick rubric pass and a fact-check take minutes and protect both the client's credibility and your professional reputation.

content.value: Finding Clients
With a portfolio ready to show, the next step is getting it in front of the right people. There are three main channels for finding copywriting clients, each with different effort-to-reward profiles.

Freelance platforms (Upwork, Fiverr, Contra) — lower rates but steady volume. Good for building experience and reviews. Competition is high, so your portfolio and proposal quality matter more than anywhere else.

Cold outreach — you contact businesses directly with a personalized pitch. Higher effort per lead, but higher rates and stronger relationships. Best for targeting specific industries or company sizes you want to work with.

Referrals and network — the highest-converting channel, but it takes time to build. Every client you do great work for becomes a potential source of future work. This is a long game, not a starting strategy.
Writing a Cold Pitch

Freelance platforms have built-in traffic, and referrals come from past work. Cold outreach requires you to earn attention from scratch.

Cold outreach only works when the pitch is specific to the business you're contacting. Generic pitches ("I'm a copywriter, let me know if you need help") get ignored. A strong cold pitch follows a simple structure.
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/c416db2a-7668-4c96-8d7f-9cfc91f96ef7.webp

1. Specific observation: Show you've looked at their business. Reference their website, a recent campaign, or a specific page.
  2. Identified opportunity: Name one thing that could be stronger — without insulting them.
  3. Your suggestion: Suggest a concrete step, not a vague promise.
  4. Low-friction CTA: Don't ask for a contract. Ask for a conversation.

response.text:
Hi — I came across BrewBox's landing page while researching DTC coffee brands. The product photography is great, but I noticed the hero section leads with "Premium Single-Origin, Delivered Monthly," which describes the product but doesn't tell me why I'd switch from my current coffee routine.

A benefit-led headline like "Wake Up to Coffee You'll Actually Look Forward To" with a supporting line about the sourcing and freshness could give visitors a reason to stay on the page longer.

I put together a few ideas for how the full page could convert better. Want me to send them over?

Setting Your Rates

You can write a great pitch and land the client — let's talk about the prices. Pricing is one of the hardest decisions for new copywriters. The key principle: charge for the value of the output, not the time it took. A landing page that drives $50K in revenue is worth the same to the client whether it took you 2 hours or 20.
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/aa61d310-8652-4fef-905a-2e5e8c730796.webp
There are three common pricing models:

• Per-project: Fixed price for a defined deliverable (e.g., "$800 for a landing page"). Clients like the predictability. Best when the scope is clear.
  • Retainer: Monthly fee for ongoing work (e.g., "$2500/month for 8 emails + 12 social posts"). Provides stable income. Best for long-term relationships.
  • Per-word or per-hour: Common on freelance platforms, but often undervalues your work. You can use it as a starting point, but then move to a per-project basis as you build experience.

content.value: The Ethics of AI-Assisted Copywriting

Now for the most sensitive part every AI copywriter faces — ethics.

Using AI to write copy isn't cheating, but it does raise questions you need to think through. How you handle these questions defines whether clients trust you long-term.
Transparency

Should you tell clients you use AI? The answer is yes, when asked — and proactively when it's relevant. Many clients already expect AI involvement. What they care about is quality. Hiding AI use and getting caught damages trust far more than being upfront.
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/f93afce3-8244-40bb-b2e8-cb62dd888b50.webp
Ownership and Editing

AI generates raw material. You shape it with brief, framework choices, editing, and strategic thinking. The final deliverable reflects your expertise, not AI's. 

That said, never submit unedited AI output. Every piece should go through the full workflow: brief → draft → critique → rewrite.
Accuracy

AI can confidently state things that aren't true. Every claim, statistic, and brand detail in your copy must be verified. This is your responsibility. If an AI draft says "rated #1 by Consumer Reports," you confirm that before it goes to the client. The client is paying for copy they can publish — that means accuracy is non-negotiable.
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/de991f69-9e42-415e-b5b6-cedf84c393d3.webp

In this lesson, you'll learn how to build a portfolio, find and pitch your first clients, set rates that reflect the value, and navigate the ethics of AI-assisted copywriting.
Your Portfolio
A portfolio is what turns "I can write copy" into proof. Clients hire based on the work they can see. Your portfolio shows them what working with you looks like.

If you're a beginner, you can create spec work — sample projects for real or invented brands that demonstrate your skills. The exercises you've completed in this course are a starting point, but portfolio pieces need more polish and context.
Always label spec work clearly. Mark each piece as "Spec Project" or "Sample Work," so no one assumes a real brand hired or endorsed you.
